chunks: Interrupt applications in embedded systems. The question: What are some applications?
Interrupts are how a microcontroller deals with the outside world without wasting time. They handle incoming serial bytes, regular timer ticks, button presses, and fault alarms.
Between events the processor can do other work or sleep, which is what makes battery products last for years. The limit is event rate.
Very fast events overwhelm the processor, so hardware takes over.
Picture a night watchman who sleeps until a bell rings. Different bells mean different things. The fire bell outranks the doorbell, so if both ring, he handles the fire first.
Each time he wakes, he does only the quick, necessary action and writes a note for the day staff. But if bells rang a thousand times a second, he would never finish anything.

The lines show where each ISR hits the wall: a 2 microseconds ISR reaches 100% at about 430 kilohertz, a 10 microseconds ISR at about 97 kilohertz.
A sensible rule is to keep total interrupt load under about 30-50% so that main code and worst-case bursts still fit; that dictates which events need DMA.
ISR (interrupt service routine): the short function the interrupt runs. Ring buffer: a fixed-size queue.
The handler writes bytes in and the main program reads them out, so no byte is lost while the main program is busy.
Sleep and wake-up: a low-power mode where the chip does nothing until an interrupt wakes it.
DMA: hardware that moves data into memory without the processor, and interrupts only when a whole block is done.
A serial port at 115,200 baud delivers a byte every 86. 8 microseconds. A 2 microseconds handler that stores the byte in a ring buffer uses about 2. 3% of the processor.
Now a battery sensor. It sleeps at 2 microamps and wakes once a minute for 20 milliseconds at 10 milliamps. Average current is 2 plus 10 000 times (0. 02 over 60) about 5.
3 microamps, so a coin cell lasts years. But a 1 MB/s data stream would mean a million interrupts per second, so that needs DMA instead. That is the whole idea.

"Interrupts handle communication (UART/SPI/I2C bytes into ring buffers), timing (periodic ticks and fixed-rate control or ADC sampling), inputs (button or sensor data-ready pins, and waking from sleep), and faults (overcurrent, brown-out, watchdog warnings).
They keep the CPU free or asleep until something happens.
The limit is event rate: very fast streams or encoders go to DMA or timer hardware, and interrupts are used for block-level events."
